stories.headline: Two Indians among 28 green card holders charged with US election fraud
stories.title: Two Indians among 28 green card holders charged with US election fraud
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Two Indian nationals are among 28 green card holders charged with election fraud in California over alleged illegal voter registration and voting in US elections.

Two Indian nationals are among 28 green card holders charged with alleged election fraud in California, with US authorities accusing them of registering to vote despite not being American citizens and casting ballots in the November 2024 presidential election.
The US Department of Justice identified the two accused as Amandeep Kaur, 30, and Kamlesh Shah, 67, in a statement issued on Monday.
It said both had been charged with fraudulently registering as voters and voting in the 2024 US elections.
The department announced the charges as part of ‘Operation Protect the Vote’, an initiative aimed at investigating election fraud and protecting electoral integrity.
Eleven of the 28 accused were arrested during early morning raids across California, but it was not immediately clear whether Kaur and Shah were among those detained.
What are the allegations against the two Indians?
According to the Justice Department, Shah, a resident of Sacramento, registered to vote on the day of the November 2024 general election and cast his ballot that day.
Kaur, who lives in Rancho Palos Verdes and is seeking US citizenship, allegedly registered as a voter in December 2022 and voted in the November 2024 election.
The department said all 28 accused are lawful permanent residents, commonly known as green card holders.
While green card holders have legal immigration status in the US, they are not citizens and are not permitted to vote in US elections.

stories.headline: Qatar to announce new regional defence partnership amid Gulf tensions
stories.title: Qatar to announce new regional defence partnership amid Gulf tensions
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 19: Qatar will soon announce a new defence partnership with regional countries as it seeks to strengthen security cooperation amid continuing tensions in the Gulf, Qatar’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of State for Defence Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani has said. Speaking at the Global Security Forum in Doha, Sheikh Saoud said Qatar had reviewed its defence capabilities, with a focus on air defence, counter-drone measures, cybersecurity and water security, Al Jazeera reported. Emphasising cooperation among Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries, he said collaboration with the United States had strengthened regional defence capabilities. He claimed that more than 90 percent of attacks during the Iran war had been prevented through shared expertise and decades of military investment. Warning of further economic repercussions from disruptions to Gulf energy supplies, Sheikh Saoud said the impact had yet to reach its peak. “We haven’t reached the peak with respect to energy,” he said, cautioning that the consequences could become more severe in the coming days and months. He said instability in the Gulf threatened energy supplies and international trade, potentially disrupting supply chains between the East and the West. It could also affect Gulf investments in Europe and the US, as well as financial assistance provided by Gulf countries to other nations. Qatar’s Ras Laffan industrial complex, a major liquefied natural gas (LNG) production hub, was damaged in Iranian attacks in March, according to the report. On relations with Tehran, Sheikh Saoud said Qatar had maintained communication with Iran despite attacks on its territory and differences over the regional conflict. Referring to the two countries’ shared gasfield, he said they had enjoyed a relationship of trust before the attacks. “We never stop our communication,” he said, adding that contacts continued at different levels and that the two sides had reached a “common understanding”.

stories.headline: Ladakh and Delhi Should Forge Strategic Solidarity
stories.title: Ladakh and Delhi Should Forge Strategic Solidarity
stories.summary: It is absolutely clear that the Centre will not give Ladakh what it has not given to Jammu and Kashmir after the two regions were separated from each other in August 2019. This separation followed the reorganization of the State, through which they had been tied together since the era of the Dogra rulers. The talks between the Ladakh leadership and the Centre have not reached a fair conclusion, and it does not seem that a mutually acceptable draft will be ready anytime soon. This reality stems from the way negotiations have shaped up in recent months. Attempts to untangle the contentious issues have proved futile so far. It is a given that negotiations of this nature—where local aspirations are weighed against overall national security concerns and strategic objectives—take time. There is no scope for rushing through things when high national stakes are involved. The International Dimension Usually, Ladakh is viewed as a region cradled between borders with China and Pakistan, alongside the Pakistan-occupied territories of the erstwhile princely state of Jammu and Kashmir that acceded to India in October 1947. However, it has other international dimensions that are rarely spoken of. The Pakistani invasion of Jammu and Kashmir in October 1947 and the subsequent war that lasted well into 1948 affected Ladakh just as much as Kashmir. Its international dimensions have surfaced time and again. There are at least two recorded facts in post-independence history that highlight this: The 1999 Kargil War: This conflict demonstrated how Pakistan, after declaring itself a nuclear power in May 1998, mounted intrusions into this side of the Line of Control (LoC). International powers were keenly interested in the outcome and counseled restraint. While the United States saw the flare-up in Kargil as a sign of Kashmir becoming a flashpoint for an Indo-Pak nuclear war, Ladakh at the time was part of the Kashmir Division within Jammu and Kashmir—despite being ethically, geographically, and topographically an altogether different entity. The 2020 Standoff: More recently, China gathered its troops along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in April–May 2020 and instigated the Galwan Valley clashes in June 2020. The impact of this is still felt today, even though attempts continue to relegate the episode to the margins of history. During the tense military standoff between India and China in eastern Ladakh, which lasted for over four and a half years, the United States and other Western nations—with their own strategic goals against China—offered support and intervention, much like they did during the Kargil War. India spurned these offers, stating it was capable of handling the crisis on its own, and it ultimately did so. Ongoing Geopolitical Challenges This success, however, has not kept the region out of the international spotlight. The Galwan Valley clashes left lasting imprints on the mountains. Furthermore, any doubts about Chinese intentions following the renewed China-India bonhomie in October 2024 were cleared when Beijing declared that it does not recognize the “so-called Union Territory of Ladakh” and made several uncharitable remarks. India challenged the Chinese contention and replied in an appropriately suitable diplomatic language, but that does not change how China views this region and its positioning. The best answer to all these international and strategic concerns can be provided by the Centre alone. The Ladakh leadership knows well that only the Centre can handle a crisis of such magnitude, which also occasionally reflects on the internal situation. Therefore, it is incumbent upon them to draw a line regarding their demands. These calls for an understanding of real-time issues may be defined by mutual trust, but the fact remains that robust strategic solidarity is a national security necessity to meet the challenges strewn across the border. The changing global geopolitical order has created a whirlpool of challenges for India. These cover all regions, especially border areas sharing a hostile neighborhood. These shadows on strategic regions cannot be wished away, whether in the North-East, Kashmir, or Ladakh. Strategic solidarity must be unconditional. Lessons from Recent Unrest A fair assessment of the ongoing talks can be traced to what happened on September 24, 2025, when an unfortunate incident left four dead and several others wounded. It was only after violence hit the streets of Leh that the gravity of the situation was fully understood. There was a lesson in that: unfortunate incidents tend to occur when vested interests exploit the public gaps created by delaying the dialogue process. There should be a greater understanding of these issues, and they must be responded to with a sensitive narrative. If sensitivity and strategic necessity are fundamental requirements, then the people’s aspirations should be taken on board in a timely manner. The talks should move beyond the technicalities that Buddhists in Ladakh should simply be satisfied because they were given the UT status they had agitated for over decades. Indeed, it was a failure on the part of the Ladakhi leadership, particularly the Buddhists, that they did not clarify what specific powers they expected alongside UT status. They were simply interested in achieving UT status for two primary reasons: To showcase themselves as the ultimate paragons of Indian nationalism. To secure a secession from Kashmir—which at the time was a hotbed of terrorism—and present it as an act of nationalism. Conversely, Kargil and its population were viewed as a different people due to their strong ties with Kashmir, essentially owing to religious affinity, as both Kargil and Kashmir are overwhelmingly Muslim-majority areas. The Path Forward UT status was thought to be the best way to achieve these local objectives, and the Centre delivered exactly what it was asked for. The demands for statehood, the Sixth Schedule, and other constitutional safeguards for their land, culture, and traditions were only flagged after leadership realized that the administration within the UT setup did not match their expectations. They began weighing the pros and cons of whether they were better off with the state of J&K or under the current UT system. Now is the time to move on. The leadership should sit down together and draft a roadmap that upholds strategic solidarity. There should not be a selective approach. The path forward must be completely in sync with local aspirations and national security necessities.

stories.headline: Kashmir Golf Club holds AGM after 14-year gap
stories.title: Kashmir Golf Club holds AGM after 14-year gap
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 19: The Kashmir Golf Club held its 26th annual general meeting (AGM) and elections on Monday after a gap of 14 years, with the exercise aimed at restoring the historic club to its former glory and putting an elected executive body in place to manage its affairs. Haris Handoo, Secretary of the Royal Springs Golf Course (RSGC) and Administrator of the Kashmir Golf Club (KGC), said the club’s previous AGM was held in 2012. “Since the elected government took office in 2024, it was decided that an elected body should be put in place,” Handoo said. The election is being held to elect four members to the club’s 10-member executive committee. Five members will be nominated by the club’s president, Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, while the Chief Secretary will head the committee. Handoo said the formation of the executive body would enable club members to prioritise development works, improve maintenance and upgrade facilities at the historic venue. “Kashmir Golf Club needs to be restored to its pristine glory. It is one of the oldest golf clubs in India, second only to Kolkata,” he said, adding that the focus would be on improving the turf and other club facilities. The government has already sanctioned Rs 2 crore under the CAPEX budget for the construction of a new club building, Handoo said. The club has 525 permanent members, and officials were expecting around 60 per cent voter turnout. Voting and the announcement of results were scheduled for the same day. Handoo, who was assigned the additional charge of KGC administrator, said the election was being conducted under the control and supervision of the government, with senior member Justice Muzaffar Jaan appointed as the returning officer. He expressed hope that the club could regain its former standing within a year, with an elected body taking responsibility for identifying priorities and overseeing its functioning. “Once the reins are handed over to the members themselves, they will be able to decide the priority works and how the club should be maintained,” he said. Handoo added that golfing activities at KGC had diminished since the establishment of the Royal Springs Golf Course. The club recently hosted a caddies’ tournament, and efforts would be made to revive its independent golfing activities and organise more tournaments. He said the aim was to ensure that the historic club continued to live up to its reputation and function as an active golfing venue. Following the conclusion of elections, Advisor to the Chief Minister Nasir Aslam Wani felicitated the newly elected members of the Executive Committee of Kashmir Golf Club (KGC) at the Sher-i-Kashmir International Convention Centre (SKICC), Srinagar. Chief Minister, president of the Club, had nominated Advisor Nasir Aslam Wani to preside over the Annual General Meeting of the Kashmir Golf Club. Former Chief Minister Dr Farooq Abdullah, MLA Gulmarg Pirzada Farooq Shah, Chief Secretary Atal Dulloo who is the chairman of the Executive Committee and other club members were present on the occasion. Congratulating the newly elected members, the Advisor described Kashmir Golf Club as a prestigious institution with a distinguished place in the history of golf in the country. He noted that the elections, held after a gap of 14 years, marked an important step towards strengthening the club’s administration and restoring its facilities. The Advisor also announced that funds amounting to Rs 2 crore have been earmarked for rebuilding the clubhouse.

stories.headline: Committed to fight for restoration of Articles 370, 35A, statehood: NC
stories.title: Committed to fight for restoration of Articles 370, 35A, statehood: NC
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 19: The Jammu and Kashmir National Conference President Dr Farooq Abdullah Monday presided over a workers’ convention in the Arwah area of Beerwah constituency. The convention was organised by Beerwah MLA Dr Shafi Ahmad Wani. The convention, as per a party statement, was attended by Provincial President Showkat Ahmad Mir, Central Zone President and Chadoora MLA Ali Mohammad Dar, Budgam District President Ghulam Nabi Bhat, block presidents, constituency presidents, mohalla presidents, delegates and party workers. Addressing the convention, Dr Farooq reiterated the National Conference’s unwavering commitment to fight for the restoration of Jammu and Kashmir’s special constitutional status, Articles 370 and 35A, and full statehood. He said that before the abrogation of Article 370 on August 5, 2019, the Supreme Court, in two earlier hearings, had upheld the provision’s permanent status and described it as a permanent provision of the Constitution of India. He asserted that the National Conference would continue its struggle for the restoration of Jammu and Kashmir’s constitutional rights and special status. Highlighting the historic contributions of the National Conference, Dr Farooq said that the party’s revolutionary and historic initiatives had paved the way for land reforms, enabling poor and marginalised farmers and cultivators to acquire ownership rights over land. He said that it was also due to the National Conference that the light of education reached every household in Jammu and Kashmir, with the literacy rate rising from 6 per cent to nearly 82 per cent today. He added that the party’s role in establishing and strengthening fundamental, constitutional and democratic institutions, as well as essential infrastructure, remained unforgettable. Dr Farooq Abdullah said that repeated attempts and conspiracies had been made over the past several decades to weaken the National Conference, but with the unwavering support of the people and the grace of Almighty Allah, the party had overcome every challenge. He asserted that as long as the people stood firmly with the National Conference, no force could undermine its political strength. Targeting the PDP, Dr Farooq Abdullah said that the hardships endured by the people of Jammu and Kashmir over the past several years were a consequence of the PDP’s actions. He said that the National Conference had announced unconditional support to the PDP in 2014 and warned it against bringing the BJP to Jammu and Kashmir, cautioning that the party would wreak havoc in the region. However, he said, the PDP ignored the warning and pushed the state towards destruction. Had the PDP not brought the BJP to Jammu and Kashmir, Article 370 would not have been abrogated, he added. He described the Supreme Court’s 2024 judgment on Article 370 as entirely wrong, arguing that the same court had upheld the provision on two earlier occasions and stated that it had acquired permanent status under the Constitution of India. “Almighty Allah is watching everything. We need only to exercise patience and restraint. Oppression may last for a while, but it cannot continue forever. Allah will certainly bring oppression to an end, and injustice will be eradicated,” he said. “The winds of change have begun to blow, and they are gathering speed.” Dr Farooq Abdullah said that the people of Jammu and Kashmir were seeking their rightful due. He recalled that promises had been made regarding delimitation, elections and the restoration of statehood following the elections. “Where have those promises gone? Why has statehood still not been restored even after two years?” he asked. He said that, in January this year, National Conference Members of Parliament had met the Union Home Minister in New Delhi, where the latter had assured them that business rules would be provided immediately to clarify the respective powers of the Lieutenant Governor and the elected government. However, he said, even after ten months, the promised business rules remained nowhere in sight. He said those in power are relying on false promises and deception. “Allah’s justice may be delayed, but it is never denied. These circumstances will not last forever, and the people of Jammu and Kashmir will certainly receive their rightful due,” he said. He stressed the need for party workers to remain united, strengthen their ranks and foil the nefarious designs and conspiracies of their adversaries. Speaking about the current development scenario, Dr Farooq Abdullah said that the government led by Chief Minister Omar Abdullah was utilising all available resources to accelerate development across Jammu and Kashmir despite the most challenging circumstances. He said that every possible effort was being made to provide relief to the people. The initiation of several development projects in different parts of Jammu and Kashmir, including Beerwah constituency, reflected a new phase of progress, he added. In his address, Beerwah MLA Dr Shafi Ahmad Wani highlighted the ongoing development initiatives in the constituency. He said that substantial funds had been released for various projects and that numerous works had been initiated to improve local infrastructure and public amenities. He asserted that Beerwah was moving towards a new phase of development and reaffirmed his commitment to resolving all pending issues faced by the constituency. At the conclusion of the convention, party leaders reiterated their commitment to public service, inclusive development and the protection of Jammu and Kashmir’s constitutional rights. They expressed confidence that the National Conference would continue to enjoy the support of the people in the future. Youth National Conference Zonal President Raees Ahmad Matoo and Zonal Secretary Mohammad Ashraf Matoo were also present on the occasion.

Dr Farooq Abdullah said that repeated attempts and conspiracies had been made over the past several decades to weaken the National Conference, but with the unwavering support of the people and the grace of Almighty Allah, the party had overcome every challenge.
He asserted that as long as the people stood firmly with the National Conference, no force could undermine its political strength.
Targeting the PDP, Dr Farooq Abdullah said that the hardships endured by the people of Jammu and Kashmir over the past several years were a consequence of the PDP’s actions.

He said that the National Conference had announced unconditional support to the PDP in 2014 and warned it against bringing the BJP to Jammu and Kashmir, cautioning that the party would wreak havoc in the region.
However, he said, the PDP ignored the warning and pushed the state towards destruction.
Had the PDP not brought the BJP to Jammu and Kashmir, Article 370 would not have been abrogated, he added.

He described the Supreme Court’s 2024 judgment on Article 370 as entirely wrong, arguing that the same court had upheld the provision on two earlier occasions and stated that it had acquired permanent status under the Constitution of India.
“Almighty Allah is watching everything.
We need only to exercise patience and restraint.
Oppression may last for a while, but it cannot continue forever.

“The winds of change have begun to blow, and they are gathering speed.” Dr Farooq Abdullah said that the people of Jammu and Kashmir were seeking their rightful due.

stories.headline: Beyond Resignations
stories.title: Beyond Resignations
stories.summary: Whenever a political controversy erupts in India, one demand frequently takes centre stage: the resignation of the minister or public official concerned. But what happens after that resignation? Does the system change, are the loopholes removed, and is there any guarantee that the same problem will not arise again? A political movement should be judged not merely by whom it removes from office, but by what it changes in law. If a movement succeeds in securing a resignation but fails to correct the institutional weaknesses responsible for the controversy, it may have changed the individual without changing the system. India’s political movements need to make politicians, ministers, former bureaucrats, former judges, and other persons holding constitutional and non- constitutional positions accountable for their acts of omission and commission. The objective should not merely be to demand resignations, but to establish laws that ensure accountability and prevent the recurrence of institutional failures. Demanding resignations through political protests is like a mouse trying to make a cat smile. It may attract attention but it does little to address the structural problems within the system. Replacing one individual with another without correcting the loopholes that allowed the problem to arise, offers no lasting solution. The colonial character of Indian administration continues to raise questions about the relationship between public authority, political influence, and institutional independence. One important concern is the practice of placing favoured bureaucrats in prestigious positions after retirement. When appointments appear to reward political connections rather than transparent and objective criteria, public confidence in institutions may suffer. This is why appropriate legal safeguards are necessary. Transparent selection procedures, clear eligibility criteria, disclosure of potential conflicts of interest, and suitable restrictions where justified can help protect institutional independence. Similar safeguards should be considered wherever post-retirement appointments risk creating conflicts between public duties and private or political interests. International experiences demonstrate that countries adopt different approaches to regulating post-retirement appointments. While their legal frameworks vary, the objective is not necessarily to impose a blanket ban on such appointments, but to establish a transparent and accountable statutory framework. South Korea, for instance, imposes restrictions on certain retired officials where their prospective employment is closely connected with their previous official responsibilities. Singapore, meanwhile, provides a framework for public appointments that emphasises constitutional qualifications, relevant experience, and prescribed appointment procedures. These examples highlight the importance of clear eligibility criteria, safeguards against conflicts of interest, recorded reasons for selection, and transparent appointment procedures. Retirement should not create unchecked opportunities for political favouritism. The fundamental objective must be to ensure that public offices are conferred on the basis of merit, competence, and integrity, rather than being perceived as rewards for past political proximity or loyalty. The appointment of retired constitutional functionaries to influential positions must, therefore, be subjected to appropriate scrutiny. Whether it concerns a former holder of high constitutional office accepting a public position, a former Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) assuming another influential office, or a retired public official being appointed as the chairman of a public-sector bank, the process must be governed by clear legal standards and safeguards against conflicts of interest. Similarly, extensions of tenure and post-retirement appointments should be regulated through transparent, objective, and legally enforceable criteria. Ultimately, the objective is not to disqualify experienced individuals from further public service, but to ensure that their appointment does not compromise institutional independence, public confidence, or the integrity of constitutional and statutory bodies. Institutions such as the Election Commission of India, the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC), and other constitutional and statutory bodies must function independently and remain accountable under the law. The need of the hour is to strengthen the legal framework governing these institutions rather than depend solely on the goodwill or integrity of the individuals heading them. Every political movement’s success depends, to a considerable extent, on leadership, public participation, strategic adaptation, and clear organisation. A movement should serve as a vehicle for political and social change. However, when it focuses exclusively on demanding the resignation of a minister or a high-ranking official, its wider purpose risks being lost. The real causes of institutional malfunction may remain untouched, along with the deficits in knowledge, trust, integrity, and accountability that the movement seeks to address. India’s experience with the Right to Information (RTI) movement and the Anna Hazare movement offers an important lesson. The RTI movement contributed to the enactment of the Right to Information Act, 2005, which established a statutory framework for citizens to access information held by public authorities. Similarly, the Anna Hazare-led anti-corruption movement generated nationwide public pressure for a Lokpal and contributed to the political momentum surrounding the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013. These examples demonstrate how public mobilisation can help translate citizens demands into legislation. Their significance lies not simply in the protests themselves, but in the legal changes that followed. They also remind us that the enactment of a law is only the beginning. Its effective implementation, enforcement, and periodic review are equally important. Contemporary political movements must therefore identify the precise legal changes they seek. If the problem concerns political influence over appointments, the demand should be for transparent selection procedures and appropriate safeguards. If public officials are not being held accountable, the movement should demand effective oversight and enforceable rules. If an existing law is ineffective in practice, the demand should be for better implementation or necessary amendments. If public demand calls for the resignation of an elected representative, India should also consider a properly regulated Right to Recall law, enabling citizens to seek the removal of their representatives before their term ends. Such legislation must establish clear procedures, reasonable thresholds of public support, and safeguards against political misuse. After all, democracy should not end with the right to elect, it should also ensure meaningful accountability between elections. Without a clear legislative objective, a protest risks becoming an informal marketplace of competing demands, driven by public anger but lacking a coherent strategy. Charismatic leadership and mass participation may bring people together, but lasting reform requires a clearly defined objective and a practical plan to achieve it. At the same time, peaceful protest must be protected as an essential feature of Indian democracy. Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution guarantees freedom of speech and expression, while Article 19(1)(b) protects the right to assemble peaceably and without arms, subject to constitutionally permitted restrictions. These freedoms enable citizens to question public authorities, challenge existing policies, and demand changes in the law. Governments must respond to legitimate public grievances through democratic and constitutional processes. Protest organisers, in turn, should translate public concerns into clear demands that can be pursued through peaceful mobilisation, legislative advocacy, and institutional engagement. Ultimately, a political movement should not measure its success solely by the resignation of a minister or the removal of a senior official. It should also ask whether the movement has secured meaningful legal reform, strengthened institutional independence, and reduced the possibility of the same problem recurring. A resignation may bring an immediate controversy to an end, but it does not necessarily correct the institutional failure behind it. Political movements must look beyond individuals and focus on the laws, procedures, and safeguards that govern the exercise of public power. VarunTuli, Writer and Poet

stories.headline: Centre amends Ladakh Hill Councils’ structure, electoral provisions
stories.title: Centre amends Ladakh Hill Councils’ structure, electoral provisions
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 19: The Centre has amended the legal terminology, administrative structure and electoral provisions governing the Autonomous Hill Development Councils in Ladakh to align them with the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, which led to the creation of the Union Territory of Ladakh. Under the Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Councils (Amendment) Regulation, the number of elected seats in each council will be determined by the Ladakh administration, with a minimum of seven and a maximum of 24 seats. The administration can nominate up to four members from among women and non-represented communities, subject to the one-sixth limit of the population, the regulation states. The sitting Lok Sabha member representing Ladakh will be an ex-officio member of the councils constituted for each district. Each council will have a term of five years from the date appointed for its first meeting, unless dissolved earlier. The term can be extended if holding elections is considered impracticable. The regulation also replaces references to the state and governor with the Union Territory of Ladakh and Administrator, respectively. It provides that the State Election Commission for the Union Territory of Ladakh will have the superintendence, direction and control over council elections and electoral rolls. Election disputes can be taken directly to the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh through election petitions filed within 45 days of the declaration of results. The regulation defines the district areas covered under the Act to include Leh, Sham, Nubra, Changthang, Kargil, Zanskar and Drass, along with any newly created districts. The councils will have the powers of panchayats at the district level and will be deemed to be district-level panchayats for exercising powers and performing functions under the Jammu and Kashmir Panchayati Raj Act, 1989. Meanwhile, the Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA), one of the two bodies engaged in talks with the central government on Ladakh’s demands, has objected to the government’s recent decision to amend the legal terminology, administrative structure and electoral provisions governing the Autonomous Hill Development Councils in the Union Territory. KDA co-chairman Sajad Hussain Kargili termed the development as deeply problematic amid the ongoing talks between Ladakh leaders and the Ministry of Home Affairs. “At a time when talks are ongoing to negotiate a settlement for Ladakh, including demands for constitutional status and stronger protections for the Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council (LAHDCs), it is deeply problematic that the government has chosen to make substantial changes to the composition, powers and functioning of these Councils without consulting the people and stakeholders of Ladakh,” Sajad Kargili, co-chairman of KDA, wrote on X. “These changes directly affect the institutions through which local self-government is exercised, making consultation especially important when the future of Ladakh’s political and constitutional arrangements remains under discussion,” he said, adding, “The government is effectively changing the institutional framework that these negotiations are meant to address, while giving the Union Territory administration greater control over the composition and functioning of the Councils.” “This raises serious questions about the government’s commitment to the ongoing dialogue and whether the eventual settlement will secure meaningful autonomy for Ladakh or leave its representative institutions subject to executive discretion,” Kargili said.

stories.headline: The selective lens of history
stories.title: The selective lens of history
stories.summary: Advocate Sunil Sethi’s recent analysis in Greater Kashmir, “NC and Congress: History of political misadventures,” rightly demands a painful, honest reckoning with Jammu and Kashmir’s past. He correctly asserts that when short-term power overrides democratic integrity, institutional damage endures for generations. The historical trajectory he charts, from the forced reversals of the 1975 Accord to the catastrophic manipulation of the 1987 elections, consists of undeniable blunders for which the National Conference and Congress must answer. Yet, an honest reckoning cannot be selective. If history demands true political accountability rather than convenient explanations, the lens of scrutiny must turn with equal force towards the BJP. The present establishment routinely treats its own record as an exception to the rule. However, for over two decades, BJP has embedded itself within the region’s political matrix, engaging in the exact brand of opportunistic accommodations and realpolitik it decries in its predecessors. While new highways, tunnels, and road networks are visible achievements, they serve as a glossy facade. Beneath this manufactured normalcy, Jammu and Kashmir remains caught in a volatile, evolving conflict marked by shifting security threats, unprecedented societal crises, and a total democratic deficit. Central to the current establishment’s narrative is its routine bragging over record-breaking tourist footprints. Conflating recreational footfall with genuine, structural peace is a deceptive illusion. Tourists visit under the heavily armed protection of omnipresent security cordons, passing through a landscape dotted with bunkers and checkpoints. Tourism is a commercial transaction facilitated by temporary stability; it is not an indicator of a resolved political conflict or a reconciled populace. The region has witnessed a shivering increase in targeted assassinations specifically designed to engineer demographic fear. Elusive, untraceable hybrid cells have systematically executed vulnerable populations, including minority Kashmiri Pandits, grassroots political workers, and non-local migrant laborers. Simultaneously, strategic stabilization of the past has disintegrated with dramatic, violent reactivation of the Jammu division. Highly trained foreign mercenaries have systematically shifted the theater of conflict utilizing the rugged terrains of Udhampur, Rajouri, Poonch, and Kathua to launch lethal operations. From regular ambushes on security installations to the brutal attack on pilgrims in Reasi, Jammu is effectively boiled all over again, proving that valley containment has simply pushed a lethal conflict into previously cleared territories. Beyond the immediate threat of gunfire lies an unprecedented socio-economic catastrophe: J&K’s worst-ever drug influx. There has been a lethal surge of high-potency synthetic opioids, primarily intravenous heroin, locally known as “Chitta”. Driven extensively by cross-border drone smuggling networks that use narco-terrorism to fund insurgent infrastructure, this epidemic has swept up an estimated 1 to 1.35 million users. It is systematically hollowing out an entire generation of youth, tearing the social order apart far faster than the UT’s limited rehabilitation infrastructure can manage. The BJP cannot distance itself from the very matrix of power it claims to have dismantled. The party’s own record is defined by the “politics of contradiction.” In 1999, under the Vajpayee-led NDA, it readily inducted Omar Abdullah, the premier face of the dynastic order it lambasts, into the Union Cabinet. In 2015, the quest for power culminated in a highly contradictory coalition with PDP, for which the BJP willfully shelved its foundational demands under a mutually convenient “Agenda of Alliance.” The ultimate irony manifested when, after placing harsh curbs on these regional dynasts post-August 2019 and branding them as untrustworthy, the Prime Minister’s Office invited these very same untrustworthy leaders for political consultations in New Delhi. This exposes a recurring truth: when it suits BJP, yesterday’s adversary instantly becomes today’s indispensable partner. SethiJi is entirely correct that political accountability concerns whether decisions taken by those exercising power strengthened or weakened the institutions entrusted to them. Congress and the National Conference must face historical scrutiny for their past conduct. However, BJP cannot escape the consequences of its own governance since 1999, 2015, and the post-2019 era of direct rule. When a state boasts of record tourist numbers but cannot guarantee the safety of pilgrims on its hills, and when it showcases infrastructure while its youth are destroyed by an unchecked drug epidemic, it is not an erasure of the conundrum. It is merely the continuation of political experimentation by different means. History demands symmetric accountability, and the current rulers of New Delhi are as much a part of this boiling conundrum as the dynasts they seek to replace. Lalit Aditya Pandit, Kashmiri Pandit Activist, Columnist, Journalist with JK Patrika.

However, BJP cannot escape the consequences of its own governance since 1999, 2015, and the post-2019 era of direct rule.

When a state boasts of record tourist numbers but cannot guarantee the safety of pilgrims on its hills, and when it showcases infrastructure while its youth are destroyed by an unchecked drug epidemic, it is not an erasure of the conundrum.
It is merely the continuation of political experimentation by different means.
History demands symmetric accountability, and the current rulers of New Delhi are as much a part of this boiling conundrum as the dynasts they seek to replace.
Lalit Aditya Pandit, Kashmiri Pandit Activist, Columnist, Journalist with JK Patrika.
